examples.question_text: A particle moves in a straight line with displacement $x(t)=2t^3-6t^2+5t-3$ metres, where $t\ge0$ is measured in seconds. Find its velocity and acceleration functions, its initial displacement, velocity and acceleration, and its velocity and acceleration at $t=2$.
examples.solution_text:
Differentiate displacement once for velocity and twice for acceleration.
$\begin{align*}v(t)&=\dot{x}(t)=6t^2-12t+5\\a(t)&=\ddot{x}(t)=12t-12\end{align*}$
Initial values use $t=0$.
$\begin{align*}x(0)&=-3\text{ m}\\v(0)&=5\text{ m/s}\\a(0)&=-12\text{ m/s}^2\end{align*}$
At $t=2$:
$\begin{align*}v(2)&=6(2)^2-12(2)+5\\&=5\text{ m/s}\\a(2)&=12(2)-12\\&=12\text{ m/s}^2\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: A particle has displacement $x(t)=2\cos 4t$ metres, where $t\ge0$ is measured in seconds. Find its velocity and acceleration functions, then evaluate both at $t=\pi/8$.
examples.solution_text:
Use the chain rule at each differentiation.
$\begin{align*}v(t)&=\dot{x}(t)=-8\sin 4t\\a(t)&=\ddot{x}(t)=-32\cos 4t\end{align*}$
At $t=\pi/8$, the angle is $4t=\pi/2$.
$\begin{align*}v(\pi/8)&=-8\sin(\pi/2)\\&=-8\text{ m/s}\\a(\pi/8)&=-32\cos(\pi/2)\\&=0\text{ m/s}^2\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: A particle has displacement $x(t)=t^2e^{-2t}$ metres, where $t\ge0$ is measured in seconds. Find its velocity and acceleration as functions of time.
examples.solution_text:
Apply the product rule, using $\dfrac{d}{dt}e^{-2t}=-2e^{-2t}$.
$\begin{align*}v(t)&=2te^{-2t}-2t^2e^{-2t}\\&=(2t-2t^2)e^{-2t}\end{align*}$
Differentiate the velocity using the product rule again.
$\begin{align*}a(t)&=(2-4t)e^{-2t}-2(2t-2t^2)e^{-2t}\\&=(4t^2-8t+2)e^{-2t}\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: A particle has displacement $x(t)=1+4\ln(t+2)$ metres, where $t\ge0$ is measured in seconds. Find its initial velocity and initial acceleration.
A particle moves in a straight line with displacement $x(t)=t^3-9t^2+15t+2$ metres for $t\ge0$, with $t$ in seconds. Find every time it is at rest and its acceleration at each of those times.
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{align*}v(t)&=3t^2-18t+15\\a(t)&=6t-18\end{align*}$
At rest, $v(t)=0$.
$\begin{align*}3t^2-18t+15&=0\\3(t-1)(t-5)&=0\end{align*}$
Both times satisfy $t\ge0$: $t=1\text{ s}$ and $t=5\text{ s}$.
$\begin{align*}a(1)&=6(1)-18\\&=-12\text{ m/s}^2\\a(5)&=6(5)-18\\&=12\text{ m/s}^2\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: A particle has displacement $x(t)=3\sin 3t$ metres for $0\le t\le2\pi/3$, with $t$ in seconds. Find every time the particle is at rest.
examples.solution_text:
$v(t)=9\cos 3t$.
At rest, $v(t)=0$, so $\cos 3t=0$. The time restriction gives $0\le3t\le2\pi$.
$\begin{align*}3t&=\frac{\pi}{2}\quad\text{or}\quad\frac{3\pi}{2}\\t&=\frac{\pi}{6}\quad\text{or}\quad\frac{\pi}{2}\end{align*}$
The particle is at rest at $t=\pi/6\text{ s}$ and $t=\pi/2\text{ s}$.

examples.question_text: A particle has displacement $x(t)=t^3-6t^2+7t+4$ metres for $t\ge0$, with $t$ in seconds. Find its velocity when its acceleration is $6\text{ m/s}^2$.
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{align*}v(t)&=3t^2-12t+7\\a(t)&=6t-12\end{align*}$
Find the time when $a(t)=6$.
$\begin{align*}6t-12&=6\\6t&=18\\t&=3\end{align*}$
Substitute this time into velocity.
$\begin{align*}v(3)&=3(3)^2-12(3)+7\\&=27-36+7\\&=-2\text{ m/s}\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: A particle has displacement $x(t)=t^3-6t^2-15t+8$ metres for $t\ge0$, with $t$ in seconds. Find its displacement at the instant it is at rest.
A particle has displacement $x(t)=t+\dfrac{9}{t+1}$ metres for $t\ge0$, with $t$ in seconds. Find its acceleration at the instant it is at rest.
examples.solution_text:
Write the reciprocal term as $9(t+1)^{-1}$ before differentiating.
$\begin{align*}v(t)&=1-9(t+1)^{-2}\\a(t)&=18(t+1)^{-3}\end{align*}$
At rest, $v(t)=0$.
$\begin{align*}1-\frac{9}{(t+1)^2}&=0\\(t+1)^2&=9\end{align*}$
Since $t\ge0$, $t+1$ is positive. Thus $t+1=3$ and $t=2\text{ s}$.
$\begin{align*}a(2)&=\frac{18}{3^3}\\&=\frac{2}{3}\text{ m/s}^2\end{align*}$

examples.question_text:
For each displacement function, differentiate twice and show the stated relationship. Displacement is in metres and $t\ge0$ is in seconds.
(a) $x(t)=4\cos 3t$: show that $\ddot{x}=-9x$.
(b) $x(t)=2e^{-3t}$: show that $\ddot{x}=9x$.

examples.derivation: Differentiating gives v(t)=6t²−12t+5 and a(t)=12t−12. At t=0, displacement is −3 m, velocity is 5 m/s and acceleration is −12 m/s². At t=2, velocity is 24−24+5=5 m/s and acceleration is 24−12=12 m/s².
The chain rule gives v(t)=−8 sin(4t) and a(t)=−32 cos(4t). At t=π/8, 4t=π/2, giving velocity −8 m/s and acceleration 0 m/s².
The product rule gives v(t)=(2t−2t²)e^(−2t). Differentiating again gives [(2−4t)−2(2t−2t²)]e^(−2t)=(4t²−8t+2)e^(−2t).
Differentiation gives v(t)=4/(t+2) and a(t)=−4/(t+2)². Substituting t=0 gives initial velocity 2 m/s and initial acceleration −1 m/s².
Velocity is 3t²−18t+15=3(t−1)(t−5), so the admissible rest times are 1 s and 5 s. Acceleration is 6t−18, giving −12 m/s² and 12 m/s² respectively.
Velocity is 9 cos(3t). On 0≤3t≤2π, its zeros occur at 3t=π/2 and 3π/2. Thus all rest times are π/6 s and π/2 s.
Velocity is 3t²−12t+7 and acceleration is 6t−12. Setting acceleration to 6 gives t=3 s. The velocity is then 27−36+7=−2 m/s.
Velocity is 3t²−12t−15=3(t−5)(t+1). Only t=5 satisfies t≥0. Substitution into displacement gives 125−150−75+8=−92 m.
Velocity is 1−9/(t+1)² and acceleration is 18/(t+1)³. Rest requires (t+1)²=9. Since t≥0, t+1=3 and t=2 s. Acceleration is 18/27=2/3 m/s².
For (a), successive derivatives are −12 sin(3t) and −36 cos(3t)=−9x. For (b), successive derivatives are −6e^(−3t) and 18e^(−3t)=9x.
